# **Proposal for a ToIP Verifiable Agent Relationship Architecture (Revised)**

**GREEN TEXT shows locations of revisions. Some have been blackened as accepted already.** 

## **A Unified Stack for Agent Interaction: Relationship Architecture from [Fiduciary Preferences](https://docs.google.com/document/u/0/d/1DGCo5GkULqHUrYv7ZeswY9gMc73CKqFhws6lhwka3ks/edit) integrated with TSP, TSP-Enabled Agents, Trust Tasks and other Verifiable Trust Infrastructure**

 by Stephen Vitka, of [Kwaai.ai](http://kwaai.ai), [stephen.vitka@gmail.com](mailto:stephen.vitka@gmail.com)   V0.3, July‘26

## **Executive Summary**

I propose that Trust Over IP develop a **Verifiable Agent Relationship Architecture** that brings together several complementary ToIP efforts with my relational and agreement model developed in [Fiduciary Preferences](https://docs.google.com/document/u/0/d/1DGCo5GkULqHUrYv7ZeswY9gMc73CKqFhws6lhwka3ks/edit) in partnership with the [Glianet Alliance](http://glianetalliance.org). This work would proceed in the existing workgroups where the component protocols below are already being pursued. 

The architecture would integrate:

* the Trust Spanning Protocol;  
* TSP-Enabled AI Agent Protocols;  
* the Trust Tasks Framework and registry;  
* Verifiable Relationship Credentials;  
* RCards;  
* Verifiable Trust Agents and Verifiable Trust Communities;  
* other verifiable credentials, attestations, and trust registries;  
* my Verifiable Relationship Records and Relationship Views.

The goal is to enable AI agents to participate in relationships that remain intelligible, governed, verifiable, and correctable beyond the lifetime of any particular message, session, task, or Live Agent instantiation inside a model. 

Existing agent systems are generally organized around temporary interactions. An agent discovers another agent or tool, exchanges messages, performs a task, and returns a result. Some implementations preserve task or conversation state, but the interaction itself remains the principal unit.

Persistent Agent Roles and the Live Agents that temporarily populate them require a durable local container: the Role Record. When an Agent Role enters an external relationship, relationship-bearing portions of its Role Record become cryptographically connected to data, attestations, receipts, pointers, commitments, and evidence held by counterparties and other authorized participants. Together, those distributed materials form the Verifiable Relationship Record.

A verifiable relationship may contain many interactions, tasks, agreements, authorizations, capabilities, data flows, reviews, attestations, complaints, amendments, and periods of inactivity. It may survive the replacement of the Live Agent, model, tool, service provider, communication channel, or local implementation. Its continuing identity and state should not depend on the hidden memory of a model or the continued availability of a particular platform.

The architecture integrates nine elements distributed across the canonical four-layer ToIP Technology Stack, the parallel Governance Stack, two cross-layer bands for relational data and persistent state, and an accountable-agent implementation envelope:

* **TSP(Trust Spanning Protocol)** supplies the Layer 2 secure relationship channel.

* **Trust Tasks** supply exact, versioned Layer 3 protocol operations.

* **Relationship Views** support human- and machine-facing interaction at Layer 4\.

* The **Verifiable Trust Agent** subsystem supplies protected cryptographic and trust-support functions at Layer 1\.

* **Verifiable Trust Communities** supply governance, assurance, certification, recognition, and recourse through the parallel Governance Stack.

* **Agent RCards** describe participating agents in the relational-data band.

* **Verifiable Relationship Credentials** provide thin, portable evidence of recognized, typed relationship edges in the relational-data band.

* **Role Records** preserve each **Agent Role**’s authoritative local state. Verifiable Relationship Records are logical, distributed structures assembled from relationship-bearing data and evidence held across those Role Records and by other authorized participants.

* The **TSP-Enabled Agent** and its **Controller** form an accountable-agent implementation envelope spanning all four Technology Stack layers and their governance interfaces.

Some of these architecture elements are placed primarily within one canonical layer; others are data objects, persistent relational state, governance structures, or implementation components that operate across several layers.

The pattern is:

> The Live Agent proposes; deterministic Workflows interpret, constrain, and compose; the embedded Verifiable Trust Agent subsystem protects and exercises cryptographic authority; TSP carries the resulting exact Trust Task messages; each counterparty verifies them independently; Role Records preserve each Agent Role’s authorized local state; distributed Verifiable Relationship Records preserve the externally meaningful intersection of relationship-bearing data, attestations, receipts, pointers, commitments, and evidence; typed agreement and record links preserve material context across the larger Relationship; Relationship Views make authorized portions intelligible; and Verifiable Trust Communities provide external governance and assurance.

No single component proves the legitimacy of the entire action. Legitimacy depends upon the verified conjunction of identity, role, authority, applicable agreement or other governing basis, duties, relationship state, capability, Workflow authorization, protected signing, counterparty verification, and required evidence.

**This would turn the existing ToIP components into an end-to-end architecture for agents that do not merely exchange trusted messages, but maintain accountable relationships. This architecture enables long-viewed fiduciary AI agents managing precise duties in a complex, ongoing web of relationships with both other agents and people, a model of “alignment” almost totally unimagined by the larger industry.**

## 

## **1\. Trusted Messages Are Not Yet Trusted Relationships**

TSP can establish that a message came from the controller of a particular Verifiable Identifier, that the message was not altered, and, where required, that its contents and communication metadata were protected.

A TSP-Enabled Agent can become a durable unit of authorization and accountability. It can receive delegated authority, communicate through TSP, and produce evidence tied to a persistent cryptographic identity.

Trust Tasks can define finite, interoperable units of work between parties.

These are necessary foundations, but they do not by themselves answer the larger relational questions:

* Whom does the agent represent?  
* Which beneficiary or beneficiaries does it serve?  
* Which duties constrain its conduct?  
* Which owner preferences may it act upon?  
* What authority does it possess?  
* Which exact agreement governs the action?  
* Which capabilities may be exercised?  
* What effects on non-parties must be considered?  
* What evidence must be retained?  
* What happens if the parties disagree?  
* What obligations survive completion of the immediate task?  
* How can another agent continue the relationship later?  
* How does conduct affect reputation?  
* How are mistakes corrected and harms remediated?

The answers cannot safely live only in model context, prompt text, transient protocol state, or a private database controlled by one participant.

A durable verifiable agent relationship requires an interoperable structure that links identity, authority, duty, agreement, execution, evidence, review, dispute, remediation, and current state.

The distributed Verifiable Relationship Record would serve this purpose.

## 

## **2\. Objectives**

The proposed architecture should make it possible for independently implemented agents to:

1. discover and verify one another  
2. communicate through TSP using durable and relationship-appropriate identifiers  
3. present verifiable descriptions of their roles, duties, authority, architecture, and certifications  
4. establish verifiable relationship edges as VRCs  
5. represent bilateral and multi-party relationships   
6. distinguish substantive parties, principals, beneficiaries, representatives, constitutors, witnesses, certifiers, adjudicators, community recognizers, and affected-party representatives;  
7. preserve typed context among related agreements and Verifiable Relationship Records without collapsing them into a master dossier;  
8. express and cast owner-authorized relational intents  
9. determine whether cooperation is compatible with their duties and authority  
10. identify and address material effects on outsiders  
11. negotiate and accept exact Agreement Objects  
12. obtain meaningful owner authorization where required  
13. translate legitimate authority into narrowly scoped technical capabilities  
14. execute tasks without giving generative agents direct authority over keys or actuators  
15. produce third-party-verifiable process and outcome evidence  
16. preserve relationship continuity across sessions, tasks, models, and implementations  
17. receive feedback, challenges, complaints, and dispute claims  
18. perform remediation  
19. revise, renew, suspend, or close relationships without rewriting prior history  
20. present understandable Relationship Views to authorized humans and agents  
21. participate in several trust communities without becoming subordinate to one centralized policy authority  
22. maintain a stable Agent Role identity while keys, models, Workflows, devices, and TSP-Enabled Agent implementations change;  
23. verify historical key state, rotation, recovery, and controller succession;  
24. distribute authenticated state changes to authorized followers without making notification infrastructure the trust root;  
25. prove which exact data every relationship party formally inspected at a particular time;  
26. distinguish collective knowledge from delivery, copying, possession of ciphertext, acknowledgment, agreement, and belief;  
27. detect rollback, stale state, forks, and equivocation;  
28. recover an Agent Role and its relationships from the last defensible state.

The architecture should remain:

* transport-independent above TSP;  
* model-independent  
* implementation-independent  
* compatible with decentralized control  
* capable of selective disclosure, including zero-knowledge proofs or other data-minimizing proofs  
* resistant to model-level manipulation and capable of containing prompt or context injection and compromised or misaligned models  
* capable of long-term identity Agent Roles and relationship continuity through a series of ephemeral Live Agents  
* governed through open specifications and plural trust communities

The architecture must preserve several distinctions that ordinary agent systems frequently collapse:

* identity is not authority;  
* relationship recognition is not agreement;  
* agreement is not capability;  
* capability possession is not proof of legitimate authority;  
* community membership is not universal authorization;  
* a signed message is not proof that the correct Workflow produced it;  
* a Verifiable Relationship Credential is not the complete relationship;  
* a Verifiable Relationship Record is not necessarily identical to one agreement;  
* linkage between records does not automatically merge their governance or authorize traversal of their contents.


A consequential action is legitimate only when the relevant distinctions have been evaluated and their required relationships have been established.

## **3\. Core Concepts and Terminology**

The architecture depends upon maintaining clear boundaries among protocol operations, relational processes, local implementation, persistent state, and governance:

* A Trust Task is an exact, reusable Layer 3 protocol operation.

* A ceremony is a sequence or graph of Trust Tasks and associated local or human steps directed toward a larger relational purpose.

* An interaction pattern is a reusable abstract composition of parties, roles, Trust Tasks, and outcomes.

* A deterministic Workflow is a local implementation and enforcement process.

* An application Workflow coordinates end-to-end Layer 4 activity.

* A Verifiable Relationship Record preserves authorized persistent relational context, including agreements.

* A Verifiable Trust Community supplies governance and assurance but does not automatically own or constitute every relationship in which its members participate.

The same real-world event may engage several of these structures, but they should not be treated as interchangeable.

### **3.1 Agent Role**

An **Agent Role** is the persistent semantic role through which an agent system represents a principal, beneficiary, organization, or other accountable interest.

The Agent Role anchors:

* identity;  
* duties;  
* authority;  
* agreements;  
* certifications;  
* reputation;  
* relationship history;  
* approved Workflows;  
* Workspace configuration;  
* continuity across Live Agent instances.

The Agent Role persists even though the generative process currently operating within it may be temporary. Live agents instantiated into/by the larger Agent role may have sub-roles which are described in their prompting or by their function in a particular workflow. The execution records of those sub-agents in sub-roles are integrated into the persistent Agent Role. 

A person may maintain several associated or independent Agent Roles. The same person might have separate yet interacting Agent Roles for personal representation, financial stewardship, research collaboration, public advocacy, and membership in an organization.  The  boundary for an Agent Role is whatever makes it the most functional carrier of accountability.  Roles may be bound to humanity-proving identifiers for their associated agents to benefit from their principal's reputation, or may be pseudonymous in some arenas after proving association with a unique human to ensure equitable representation. 

### **3.2 Live Agent**

A **Live Agent** is a temporary generative process instantiated for a particular workload.

It may reason, draft, classify, explain, negotiate, and generate proposed media. It does not itself provide the persistent identity of the fiduciary party, and it should not directly control consequential actuators.

A Live Agent’s proposed action remains media until interpreted by a deterministic Workflow/ Harness 

When the Live Agent terminates, its authorized outputs and execution records persist. 

### **3.3 Deterministic Workflow**

A **deterministic Workflow** is a non-generative process whose permitted inputs, outputs, validations, state transitions, and actuator calls are defined in advance.

A Workflow may:

* select context for a Live Agent;  
* retrieve relationship state;  
* validate credentials;  
* check an Agreement Object;  
* evaluate an authority chain;  
* determine whether owner review is required;  
* validate a Trust Task schema;  
* issue or restrict a capability;  
* invoke a protected signing operation;  
* transmit a message;  
* write a permitted event to a record;  
* refuse an unsupported or unauthorized operation.

The Deterministic Workflow may use generative models as contained components for classification or interpretation, but the resulting action must still pass through deterministic validation and a closed set of permitted state transitions.

### **3.4 Workspace**

The **Workspace** is the controlled environment in which Deterministic Workflows operate.

It contains or mediates access to:

* memory, records and files;  
* policies;  
* credentials;  
* relationship state;  
* tools and actuators;  
* communication systems;  
* protected key stores;  
* audit systems;  
* capability services;  
* approved model interfaces.

The Workspace determines what the system can actually reach or change. It therefore supplies the capability boundary that makes duties and agreements operational.

### **3.5 TSP-Enabled Agent**

A **TSP-Enabled Agent**, or TEA, is the durable technical unit that participates as a TSP endpoint and to which authority and accountability must be assigned.

For most cases, a TEA is a composite bot, according to my [Taxonomy.](https://docs.google.com/document/u/0/d/1a-Rn9V4UgtXs9EYniTAyjvG93QfzzenXfUNK3nW_Sss/edit) It may include or be assembled from:

* the persistent Agent Role (which could be transferred to another upgraded TEA, providing continuity)  
* the deterministic Workflow system; the harness  
* the controlled Workspace;  
* an embedded VTA trust subsystem;  
* a TSP Gateway;  
* approved models and Live Agents;  
* memory;  
* tools;  
* actuators;  
* relationship records.

The complete composite system is the accountable actor. A Sub-TEA may be instantiated with delegated authority from a parent TEA.  Instantiated sub-TEAs leave sufficient evidence for evaluation, but their actions are ultimately the responsibility of the issuing parent TEA.

### **3.6 TEA Controller**

The TEA Controller within a TSP-Enabled Agent should be understood as the set of interwoven deterministic Workflows belonging to or authorized for the Agent Role.

The Controller mediates:

* model context;  
* memory access;  
* tool use;  
* external communication;  
* authority;  
* capability issuance;  
* signing;  
* relationship-state changes;  
* required records.

### **3.7 Agent Role Addresses and Interaction VIDs**

An Agent Role Address is the stable cryptographic identifier of a persistent Agent Role. It should remain stable across routine signing-key rotation, encryption-key rotation, model replacement, Workflow replacement, Workspace migration, and transfer to an upgraded TSP-Enabled Agent. It resolves or anchors a verifiable control and state history rather than merely naming one current public key.

An Interaction VID(Verifiable Identifier) is an identifier used for discovery, communication, or participation in a particular trust or relationship domain. Interaction VIDs may be public, pairwise, nested, routed, temporary, or relationship-specific.

A stable Agent Role Address does not itself confer authority. Authority arises from owner authorization, delegation, agreement, law, constituting action, or another legitimate authority instrument. A verifier should therefore ask separately:

* Is this the relevant Agent Role?  
* Which key state controlled it when the act was signed?  
* What authority did it possess for this act?  
* Which capability made execution possible?

Privacy-preserving proofs may establish that an Interaction VID is controlled by an Agent Role without making every Interaction VID publicly correlatable.

### **3.8 Embedded VTA Trust Subsystem**

In this proposal, a **VTA trust subsystem** refers to the **OpenVTC Verifiable Trust Agent implementation pattern:** protected VID management, key custody, policy-bound signing, key rotation, and related cryptographic operations.

The VTA is considered an embedded part of the TEA Controller’s deterministic Workflow system — to be invoked by it. Its protected keys, policies, anti-rollback data, and cryptographic state are isolated Workspace resources safe from less-trustworthy components. 

The embedded VTA should also support:

* maintaining or verifying the Agent Role’s key-control history;  
* enforcing precommitted rotation and recovery policy;  
* anchoring or verifying the current Role Record state;  
* producing authenticated state-update announcements;  
* refusing operations against stale, forked, rolled-back, or suspended state;  
* issuing cryptographic-use receipts.

**The Generative Live Agent suggests:**  
	This exact Trust Task (identified so as to be interpretable to the Deterministic Workflow)  
 	would be ideal to execute now according to my probabilistic interpretation of state.      

**The Workflow determines:**  
> This exact Trust Task is permitted by the current agreement, authority, duties, and relationship state.

**The embedded VTA determines:**  
> This authenticated Workflow is permitted to exercise this particular VID for this exact cryptographic operation.

### **3.9 Verifiable Trust Community**

A **Verifiable Trust Community**, or VTC, is a community governance and assurance layer. It reinforces and refines standards and norms, socially. 

A VTC may manage:

* its membership;  
* community roles for members; some available for only humans, some only for agents  
* governance policies;  
* preferred credential types; for admission but also member to member.  
* duty bundles for agents, pledges and guidelines for humans  
* TEA  and  component certifications; both issuing and requiring them  
* Trust Task implementation credentials; both issuing and requiring them  
* recognized witnesses, auditors, mediators, and arbitrators;  
* revocation and suspension;  
* trust-registry publication;  
* relationships with peer communities.

A VTC’s claims are evidence evaluated by an agent’s local Workflows. Their authority is modulated by the agent's (and its owner’s) sovereignty. 

### **3.10 TSP Relationship**

A **TSP Relationship** is a pairing of VIDs in which one TSP endpoint has verified another endpoint’s VID for communication. It is directional unless both endpoints have independently verified the other.

A TSP Relationship is a communication and endpoint-verification relationship. It is not the same thing as a substantive agent relationship.

A Verifiable Relationship Record may preserve the continuity of a relationship while the parties use or replace multiple TSP Relationships and VID pairs. For example, one Alice–Lab B research relationship might use:

* public Introduction VIDs for first contact;  
* private pairwise VIDs for negotiation;  
* nested VIDs for a confidential workstream;  
* replacement VIDs after key rotation or migration;  
* different VID pairs for subordinate agreements.

### 3.11 Bonding, Constituting, and Binding

The architecture distinguishes three relational functions that may occur together or separately.  
Bonding is the formation or development of a substantive relationship through mutual recognition, agreement, conduct, shared purpose, continuing expectations, or obligation. Bonding describes the relational substance created among the relevant parties.

Constituting is the act by which an authorized party, principal, quorum, community, governance authority, or other required participant makes a status, agreement, role, or relationship valid. Constitution is required only where the applicable authority or governance framework gives a participant that function.  
Binding is the act of making an event, claim, agreement, acceptance, or relationship verifiable, attributable, integrity-protected, or legible to authorized others through cryptographic or evidentiary means.

One event may perform more than one function. Acceptance of an Agreement Object may bond the parties, constitute the agreement, and cryptographically bind their acceptance. A witness may bind an event evidentially without constituting it. A Verifiable Trust Community may recognize or certify a relationship without becoming a substantive party to it.

The architecture must therefore represent relational roles explicitly. It must not collapse evidentiary witnesses, constituting authorities, certifiers, community recognizers, affected-party representatives, and substantive parties into one generic third-party role.

### **3.12 Verifiable Relationship Credential**

A **Verifiable Relationship Credential**, or VRC, supplies portable evidence of a relationship edge.

Reciprocal VRCs may show that both parties recognize the relationship. The credential can establish the relevant relationship identifiers, issuance, proof, and validity status.

The VRC should remain relatively thin. It should not contain the complete agreement, duty structure, history, performance record, or current governance state of the relationship.

A Verifiable Relationship Credential should identify the type of relationship edge it attests. It may provide evidence of an introduction, association, negotiation relationship, agreement-related relationship, delegation relationship, community relationship, or another recognized edge.  
Issuance of a Verifiable Relationship Credential does not by itself:

* create or activate an Agreement Object;  
* confer authority;  
* issue a capability;  
* establish fiduciary status;  
* demonstrate compliance;  
* authorize access to a Verifiable Relationship Record;  
* prove the entire larger Relationship;  
* make the credential issuer a constituting party.

A Verifiable Relationship Credential may be issued at different points in the relationship lifecycle. Some credentials may recognize an introduction or association before negotiation. Others may recognize entry into a ceremony, activation of an agreement, a continuing role, or a later relationship status. The credential profile must make the recognized edge and its evidentiary meaning explicit.

A VRC answers:

> Can this party provide verifiable evidence of this relationship edge?

### **3.13 Agent RCard**

An  **Agent RCard** is the agent Calling Card specified as a ToIP RCard.

It describes the participant publishing it, not the entire relationship. It may contain basic human readable description or any other data fields the publisher includes: 

It may contain or reference:

* Agent Role;  
* relevant VIDs;  
* principal and beneficiaries;  
* authority source;  
  architecture and component provenance with certification stack that also proves sufficient updates.  
* duty bundle;  
* supported Trust Tasks;  
* communication protocols;  
* capability classes;  
* limitations and prohibitions;  
* recording and disclosure rules;  
* agreement-template compatibility;  
* preferred witnesses and dispute mechanisms;  
* VTA assurance;  
* miscellaneous reputation evidence;  
* service endpoints;  
* status update \- agent’s big picture of goals, with links to granular agent history as allowed. 

Self-asserted fields must be distinguished from third-party evidence. An RCard can state that the agent possesses a certification, but the certification credential establishes the claim.

An  agent may publish a general discovery RCard and more restricted relationship-specific RCards.

### **3.14 Trust Task**

A **Trust Task** is a finite, self-contained, versioned description of verifiable work between parties.

It is transport-independent. The same task semantics may be carried through TSP regardless of the underlying network transport or local API binding.

A Trust Task should represent the **Workflow-approved relational intent**, not the Live Agent’s unfiltered output.

The Live Agent might generate:

> I recommend offering the research agent query-only access.

The deterministic Workflow must translate this into an exact task with:

* identified parties;  
* exact purpose;  
* data classes;  
* authority;  
* agreement reference;  
* duration;  
* prohibited operations;  
* approval requirements;  
* evidence requirements;  
* expiration;  
* recourse.

Only the latter may be signed and transmitted as an operative Trust Task to the VTA. 

### **3.15 Agreement Object, Authority, and Capability**

These are distinct but may be cryptographically bound together. 

An **Agreement Object** records the exact terms accepted by the parties.

An **authorization or delegation credential** establishes what an identified agent or role is legitimately permitted to do.

A **capability** supplies the technical means to perform a permitted operation.

An agreement may require a capability to be issued. An authorization may permit the agent to receive or use it. The capability makes execution technically possible.

Possessing a capability does not by itself prove authority. Accepting an agreement does not automatically create every required capability.

### **3.16 Verifiable Relationship Record**

A Verifiable Relationship Record is a logical, distributed object assembled from shared records and source-attributed attestations concerning an external relationship. Most of its underlying material lives inside the parties’ Role Records; which is where each Agent Role keeps its own copies of important shared data, receipts, commitments, private evidence, and secret-bound attestations that may later be disclosed or proved when authorized.

The Role Record is primary. A portion of a Role Record participates in the Verifiable Relationship Record when it is shared, made inspectable to all applicable parties, mutually acknowledged, cross-referenced, or intentionally bound as evidence about the external relationship. If no external party exists, there is no Verifiable Relationship Record.

Exact data is itself considered part of the Verifiable Relationship Record where it exists within at least one party’s Role Record or authorized evidence store and is inspectable by every party in the applicable party-set epoch. A visible attestation about or a pointer to data external to Role Records or agreed-upon evidence stores is part of the  Verifiable Relationship Record, but the external data is considered “linked-to” rather than contained within the Verifiable Relationship Record. Pointers and attestations may concealed inside an opaque commitment block, only the block and its provenance are shared until an authorized opening occurs.

The Verifiable Relationship Record is verifiable because claims identify their source and can be checked against signatures, content identifiers, Role Record state anchors, receipts, acknowledgments, commitments, and other evidence. Verifiability does not require every participant to agree.

One materially distinct agreement per Verifiable Relationship Record usually provides functional separation, but is not a structural requirement. A distributed Verifiable Relationship Record may represent no agreement, one agreement, several agreements intentionally governed together, or a network of typed links among agreements and relationship evidence, provided that distinct authority, duties, capabilities, lifecycle state, and privacy remain intelligible.

Relationship checkpoints may summarize accumulated collectively inspected data, visible reference objects, opaque commitments, disputes, operative agreements, and contributing Role Record states. A checkpoint is not a central master record and does not contain every party’s private evidence.

### **3.17 Relationship View and Relationship Surface**

A **Relationship View** is an authorized human- or machine-readable rendering of selected information from a **Verifiable Relationship Record**.

A principal, counterparty, witness, auditor, arbitrator, regulator, or later agent may receive a different view.

A **Relationship Surface** is the interface through which a principal reviews Relationship Views across their significant relationships.

### **3.18 Distinct Meanings of Relationship**

The term relationship is used at several architectural levels. These meanings must remain distinguishable:

* A TSP Relationship is a secure communication and endpoint-verification relationship between Verifiable Identifiers.

* A Verifiable Relationship Credential edge is portable evidence that a specified relationship edge is recognized.

* An agreement-governed relationship is the set of rights, duties, authority, expectations, and permitted actions established through one or more agreements.

* A larger substantive Relationship is the continuing relational structure that may emerge from introductions, agreements, conduct, shared history, roles, communities, and cross-referenced Verifiable Relationship Records.

* A Relationship View is an authorized presentation of selected relational information.

* A Relationship Surface is the interface through which a person or agent navigates authorized views across significant relationships.

A larger Relationship is not necessarily stored in one record. It may be represented through one Verifiable Relationship Record, through a record containing several agreements, or through a typed network of cross-referenced records and relationship evidence.

## **4\. Nine Architecture Elements Across the ToIP Technology and Governance Stacks**

The Verifiable Agent Relationship Architecture integrates nine architecture elements across the canonical four-layer Technology Stack, the parallel Governance Stack, the relational-data and persistent-state bands, and an accountable-agent implementation envelope.

**![][image1]**

### **4.1 Canonical ToIP Technology Stack**

The canonical Technology Stack remains:

* Layer 1 — Trust Support: cryptographic, identifier, key-management, integrity, status, and protected trust functions;

* Layer 2 — Trust Spanning: secure, authentic, privacy-protecting communication and endpoint relationships across trust domains;

* Layer 3 — Trust Tasks: reusable, exact, versioned protocols that perform bounded trust-building operations;

* Layer 4 — Trust Applications: human- and agent-facing applications, ceremonies, negotiation processes, review, orchestration, and domain-specific activity.

The Verifiable Trust Agent subsystem is placed primarily at Layer 1\. TSP is placed at Layer 2\. Trust Tasks are placed at Layer 3\. Relationship Views and Relationship Surfaces primarily support Layer 4 interaction.

### **4.2 Governance Stack**

The Governance Stack runs in parallel with the Technology Stack. It defines who may perform particular functions, under what authority, using which profiles, credentials, policies, assurance processes, remedies, and accountability structures.

Verifiable Trust Communities operate primarily through this Governance Stack. They may establish membership rules, recognize duty bundles, certify implementations, govern registries, recognize witnesses and adjudicators, publish status, and supply community-specific assurance.

Governance requirements are declared through governance frameworks and agreements, interpreted by local deterministic Workflows, enforced through Workspace and capability boundaries, reflected in Verifiable Trust Agent signing policy, independently evaluated by counterparties, and preserved as evidence in Verifiable Relationship Records.

### **4.3 Relational-Data and Persistent-State Bands**

Agent RCards and Verifiable Relationship Credentials belong to a relational-data band crossing the stack.

An RCard describes an agent, its role, supported protocols, claimed practices, limitations, and evidence. A Verifiable Relationship Credential provides thin, portable evidence of a typed relationship edge.

Role Records form the primary persistent-state plane for Agent Roles. Distributed Verifiable Relationship Records form an external relationship-evidence plane assembled from relationship-bearing portions of those Role Records and evidence held by other authorized participants.

A distributed Verifiable Relationship Record may represent a relationship before any agreement exists, one agreement, or multiple agreements by agreement of the relevant parties. Typed links among agreements, Role Record evidence, and related relationship structures preserve material context across the larger Relationship.

### **4.4 Accountable-Agent Implementation Envelope**

The TSP-Enabled Agent and its Controller form an implementation envelope spanning the Technology Stack and its governance interfaces.

The envelope includes:

* the persistent Agent Role;

* deterministic Workflows;

* the controlled Workspace;

* the embedded Verifiable Trust Agent subsystem;

* the TSP Gateway;

* approved models and their Live Agents;

* memory and retrieval systems;

* tools and actuators;

* credentials, capabilities, and policies;

* Role Records, distributed Verifiable Relationship Records, collective-knowledge checkpoints, and authorized Relationship Views.

This envelope describes how independently specified components are assembled into an accountable acting system.

### **4.5 End-to-End Operational Pattern**

How a Live Agent receives context is a different pattern, but starting from there; the end-to-end pattern is:

1. A Live Agent interprets context and proposes an action.

2. Workflows retrieve the relevant Agent Role, Role or Sub-Role Record checkpoint, authority, duties, distributed relationship evidence, agreements where applicable, linked context, policies, and evidence needed for the Policy Gate

3. The “Policy Gate”  Workflow determines which exact Trust Tasks and local steps are permitted or required.

4. The embedded Verifiable Trust Agent subsystem determines whether an authenticated Workflow, acting from the current defensible Role Record and historically applicable key state, may exercise the requested Agent Role Address or Interaction VID for the exact cryptographic operation.

5. The controlled Workspace limits access to data, tools, capabilities, and actuators.

6. TSP carries the resulting Trust Task message.

7. The counterparty independently verifies identity, authority, task conformance, governing context, current state, and its own duties.

8. Authorized results and evidence update the appropriate local Role or Sub-Role Records. Where they affect an external relationship, the parties create or exchange the attestations, receipts, pointers, commitments, or checkpoint effects through which the result participates in the distributed Verifiable Relationship Record.

9. Relationship Views make permitted portions intelligible to principals, counterparties, witnesses, auditors, adjudicators, and later agents.

10. Verifiable Trust Communities supply external assurance, governance, recognition, status, and recourse where applicable.

Each stage supplies evidence for the next without requiring any participant to trust the internal reasoning of another participant’s model.

![][image2]

**In the following sections the term “duty” is not used solely to indicate fiduciary duties, but also any other sort of behavioral constraints on an agent along with whatever form of verifiability, if any. We are moving towards using “obligations” to express the "duties" that can be deterministically evaluated during a “Policy Gate” check.** 

### **5.1 Discovery and Solicitation** 

An agent discovers another party through an intent, registry, recommendation, agent name, RCard, public endpoint, trust community, or other out-of-band introduction.

Discovery identifies a prospective participant. It does not prove that the participant is suitable, authorized, certified, compatible, or willing to engage.

The first active step is often a solicitation. One party announces or directs a minimal request for attention: who is requesting attention, the general class of interaction sought, why the counterparty may care, what level of engagement is requested, and which ceremony profiles may be appropriate. The soliciting party’s intent cast may be broadcast, narrowcast, directed to a known counterparty, posted within a trust community, routed through a registry, or sent privately from one agent to another.

A directed intent cast should explain why the approached party may want to engage. The solicitation explains the opportunity, the included or linked RCard identifies the requesting agent and its standing practices.

### **5.2 Calling-Card Review and Ceremony-Profile Alignment**

This stage does not yet negotiate the final agreement. It decides whether the parties will enter a negotiation ceremony at all, and under which ceremony profile.

After receiving a solicitation, likely with an included RCard, the approached agent decides whether and how to engage.

An RCard describes the participant publishing it, not the entire relationship. It may contain or reference:

● agent identity;  
● beneficiary or owner;  
● provenance of the agent and its components;  
● certification status;  
● current duty stack;  
● known forks or special covenants;  
● communication protocol support;  
● supported Trust Tasks;  
● reputation data or credentials;  
● trusted witnesses;  
● preferred arbitration venues;  
● agreement-template compatibility;  
● constraints on recording and disclosure;  
● service endpoints.

Self-asserted fields must be distinguished from third-party evidence. An RCard can state that an agent possesses a certification, but the certification credential establishes the claim.

The receiving agent reviews the solicitation and the RCard, compares the proposed interaction against its own RCard and policies, and looks for an intersection among supported methods.

The approached agent may respond at several levels:

● no response;  
● acknowledge receipt only;  
● decline without explanation;  
● decline with a limited reason code;  
● request clarification about purpose, incentive, scope, urgency, or authority;  
● request fuller RCard verification;  
● propose a compatible ceremony profile already supported by both RCards;  
● offer a counter-profile for how any further exchange must occur;  
● escalate to the owner, a group fiduciary, a trust community, a certifier, a mediator, or another authorized reviewer;  
● accept entry into a defined negotiation ceremony.

The agents may proceed when they can identify compatible communication protocols, disclosure constraints, recording rules, credential requirements, template families, witness options, arbitration venues, escalation paths, and ceremony-state semantics. If the RCards reveal a clear intersection, the agents select the compatible ceremony profile and proceed. If there is no intersection, the default result should be refusal, narrowing, or escalation.

Where the opportunity is unusually important but no existing ceremony profile overlaps, the parties may attempt a bounded ceremony-forging process. This process should identify the incompatibility, select an acceptable bridge or mediator where possible, narrow the solicitation if needed, defer sensitive disclosures, and record the failed, repaired, or newly forged profile for later template improvement.

### **5.3 TSP Relationship Formation**

Only after the parties have selected or forged an acceptable ceremony profile should they establish the TSP Relationship required for the next stage. (If a TSP Relationship already exists, there is no need to negotiate the previous steps again) 

The endpoints verify appropriate VIDs and establish one or more directional TSP Relationships.

Sensitive relationships may use pairwise, nested, routed, or relationship-specific communication to reduce correlation and metadata exposure.

The TSP Relationship supplies the secure communications path for further ceremony steps. It is not itself the substantive relationship, and it does not by itself prove authority, suitability, fiduciary status, certification, agreement, or compatibility.

### **5.4 Fuller RCard Exchange and Verification**

After a suitable ceremony profile and communications channel are available, the parties may exchange, update, or selectively disclose fuller RCards.

A fiduciary agent may publish a general discovery RCard while reserving more sensitive or relationship-specific RCards for later exchange.

The parties independently verify:

● identifiers;  
● authority credentials;  
● duty bundles;  
● certifications;  
● Workflow and Workspace assurances;  
● VTA assurance;  
● reputation evidence;  
● supported Trust Task profiles;  
● recording and disclosure constraints;  
● witness, mediator, arbitrator, or trust-community compatibility.

The RCard describes each participant. It does not prove the existence of the relationship edge.

### **5.5 Typed Verifiable Relationship Credential Formation**

Where portable evidence of a relationship edge is useful, one or more parties may issue or exchange typed Verifiable Relationship Credentials.

Credential formation is not a universally mandatory stage and need not occur at one fixed point in the lifecycle. A credential may recognize:

* an introduction;

* an association;

* entry into a negotiation ceremony;

* a role or representation relationship;

* activation of an agreement;

* an established substantive relationship;

* membership or standing within a Verifiable Trust Community;

* another explicitly defined relationship edge.

The credential must state or reference the type of edge being recognized, the parties and roles, the issuer’s authority, its validity period and status mechanism, and the meaning of issuance.  
The Verifiable Relationship Credential provides portable evidence concerning the specified edge. The RCard describes a participant. The TSP Relationship supplies secure communication between endpoints. Agreement Objects define accepted terms. Verifiable Relationship Records preserve broader authorized context and state.

A Verifiable Relationship Credential does not automatically confer authority, activate an agreement, issue a capability, authorize record access, or prove the entire larger Relationship.

### **5.6 Preliminary Relationship-Bearing Role Record State**

A party may begin recording an external contact in its own Role Record before an agreement, TSP Relationship, Verifiable Relationship Credential, or mutual acknowledgment exists. Once there is an identifiable external party and the recording party intentionally binds a solicitation, receipt, pointer, commitment, or other item as evidence concerning that external relationship, the distributed Verifiable Relationship Record begins to form.

A unilateral local interpretation does not become shared relationship data merely because it concerns another party. Unless the other party can inspect the exact data, only the source-attributed attestation, pointer, receipt, or commitment made available to it participates in the Verifiable Relationship Record.

The local Role Record state may later support negotiation and formation of one or more agreements, remain inactive without closing, or close without any agreement being formed. It must continue to distinguish the recording party’s own observations, intentions, interpretations, and private evidence from exact data inspected by all parties, mutually acknowledged state, and claims disputed by another party.

Initial relationship-bearing states may include discovered, solicited, solicitation received, RCard received or reviewed, ceremony profile under assessment, ceremony profile selected or forged, TSP channel established, Verifiable Relationship Credential pending, qualifying, negotiating, inactive, declined, expired, suspended, or closed without agreement.

The local state may preserve the purpose of contact; solicitations sent or received; RCard pointers and versions; identifiers used; ceremony profiles considered; confidentiality terms; recording permissions; evidence received; unresolved verification; refusals; and escalation decisions. It must not imply agreement, negotiation duties, mutual recognition, sensitive disclosure, consent, inspection, or acceptance unless the required events and receipts actually occurred.

If negotiations produce materially distinct agreements, the parties should normally represent them through separately governed and typed relationship evidence. If the agreements are sufficiently integrated, the parties may instead agree to govern them within the same distributed relationship structure, provided that the boundaries and effects of each agreement remain independently intelligible.

### **5.7 Relational Intent**

A Live Agent may recommend initiating, accepting, modifying, or ending a relationship.

The recommendation has no external effect until a deterministic Workflow:

1. identifies a supported intent type;  
2. retrieves the relevant Verifiable Relationship Record and authority;  
3. applies duties and policy;  
4. validates required data;  
5. determines whether owner or specialist review is required;  
6. constructs an exact Trust Task;  
7. obtains protected signing through the embedded VTA.

### **5.8 Compatibility and Consequence Considerations**

Before bargaining over detailed terms, the parties determine whether cooperation is permissible and potentially beneficial.

They evaluate:

● authority;  
● duties;  
● fiduciary preferences;  
● privacy;  
● security;  
● non-negotiable limitations;  
● reputation;  
● externalities for likely affected third parties and appropriate mitigation or inclusion;  
● approval thresholds.

### **5.9 Agreement Formation**

The agents select a template or construct an Agreement Object and negotiate exact versions through Trust Tasks.

A proposal references one immutable Agreement Object. A counterproposal creates another version. Acceptance must identify the exact live version.

The agreement should not be represented as active until its required signatures, thresholds, approvals, and activation conditions are satisfied.

### **5.10 Owner Review and Authorization**

Where required, the principal receives an understandable review packet. (While “Human in the Loop” not mentioned in other places within this Relationship Process, there are many such places, where Live Agents or Deterministic Workflows can escalate to the current user, principal or other agents as appropriate)

If the agent lacks sufficient standing authority, the owner issues an authorization tied to:

● the exact Agreement Object;  
● the permitted action;  
● the duration;  
● amendment limits;  
● re-delegation limits;  
● reporting requirements;  
● revocation terms.

### **5.11 VTA Authorization and Signing**

The Workflow submits the canonicalized Trust Task or signed-payload object to the embedded VTA trust subsystem.

The VTA checks:

● authenticated Workflow identity;  
● Agent Role permissions for using that Workflow;  
● exact Trust Task type and version tied to the permitted VID;  
● recipient;  
● expiration;  
● relevant payload restrictions;  
● local cryptographic-use policy.

The VTA signs only the approved object or digest.

### **5.12 TSP Transmission and Independent Verification**

TSP carries the Trust Task to the counterparty.

The counterparty does not merely trust the sender’s agent or Workflow interpretation, but rather independently checks:

● sender VID;  
● task type;  
● schema conformance;  
● expiration;  
● authority;  
● credentials;  
● agreement;  
● other proof;  
● current relationship state;  
● its own duties and policies.

Independent verification must keep the following questions separate:

● Does the identifier belong to or remain controlled by the claimed party?  
● Does the party occupy the claimed Agent Role?  
● Does the party possess current authority for the proposed action?  
● Is there an effective agreement or other legitimate governing basis for the action?  
● Does a linked agreement or Verifiable Relationship Record materially affect that basis?  
● Does the proposed Trust Task conform to its exact specification and profile?  
● Does the requested capability fall within the valid authority and governing terms?  
● Does the action comply with the receiving agent’s own duties, policies, and relationship state?

### **5.13 Multi-Party and Constituting-Role Verification**

Where a relationship, agreement, or Trust Task involves more than two roles, the Workflow must identify which participants are:

* substantive parties;

* principals;

* beneficiaries;

* authorized representatives;

* constitutors;

* evidentiary witnesses;

* auditors or certifiers;

* mediators or adjudicators;

* community recognizers;

* affected-party representatives.

The Workflow must verify the authority and required participation of each role independently. The presence of a third party does not by itself make that party constitutive. Conversely, a relationship or agreement must not be treated as valid where a required principal, quorum, constitutor, or affected-party representative has not participated as required.

Bilateral relationships remain valid cases and should not be forced into artificial triads. Multi-party relationships must nevertheless be represented natively rather than reconstructed as unrelated bilateral exchanges when the larger relational structure affects authority, duties, consent, or state.

### **5.14 Capability Issuance and Execution**

Once an agreement and authority are effective, the local TEA Controller may issue narrowly scoped capabilities.

Execution may use tools, APIs, MCP, A2A, or other protocols, but those operations remain governed by the relevant Role Record state, the distributed Verifiable Relationship Record, and the exact Agreement Object.

### **5.15 Attestation and Record Update**

Consequential actions produce signed process, execution, compliance, or outcome evidence.

Each party writes the resulting local state transition into its relevant Role Record. Where the transition affects the external relationship, the parties create or exchange the source attestations, content identifiers, receipts, commitments, or checkpoint updates needed to make that effect part of the distributed Verifiable Relationship Record.

### **5.16 Feedback, Challenge, and Remediation**

Parties, beneficiaries, witnesses, or affected stakeholders may submit feedback, evidence, complaints, or challenges.

The architecture distinguishes:

● feedback;  
● allegation;  
● acknowledged error;  
● disputed claim;  
● verified breach;  
● remediation;  
● corrected or overturned finding.

### **5.17 Continuation or Closure**

A later Live Agent may continue the relationship from the persistent Agent Role’s Role Record, using the distributed Verifiable Relationship Record to verify relationship-bearing shared state, counterparty acknowledgments, unresolved disputes, and externally held evidence without inheriting the private state or identity of the earlier Live Agent.

Closure records:

● termination authority;  
● surviving duties;  
● retention or deletion obligations;  
● unresolved disputes;  
● outstanding remediation;  
● successor relationships;  
● final relationship state.

## **6\. Fiduciary-Agent Ceremony Profiles Composed from Trust Tasks**

The relational lifecycle described in Fiduciary Preferences should be expressed through reusable ceremony profiles. A ceremony profile composes exact, versioned Trust Tasks with local deterministic Workflow steps, governance evaluations, human decisions, evidence requirements, and defined Verifiable Relationship Record effects.

A Trust Task is an exact Layer 3 protocol operation. A ceremony is a sequence or graph of Trust Tasks and associated steps directed toward a larger relational purpose. A simple ceremony may invoke only one Trust Task, but the concepts are not synonymous.

A ceremony profile representative of the interaction stages preceding agreement activation could include:

* solicitation and Calling-Card Review;  
* compatible ceremony-profile selection;  
* TSP Relationship formation;  
* fuller RCard exchange;  
* optional typed Verifiable Relationship Credential formation;  
* compatibility and externality review;  
* Agreement Object proposal and negotiation;  
* owner review and authorization where required;  
* exact acceptance;  
* protected signing;  
* process attestation;  
* capability activation;  
* appropriate Verifiable Relationship Record updates.

The ceremony must identify whether it is operating in a record containing no agreement, forming the first agreement in a record, adding an agreement to an existing record, or creating a separately governed but cross-referenced record.

The architecture should define requirements at four different levels.

### 

### **Generic Trust Task specification**

Each generic Trust Task specification should define:

* canonical identifier and version;  
* purpose;  
* protocol roles;  
* request, response, and evidence schemas;  
* structural preconditions;  
* permitted protocol states;  
* verifiable outcomes;  
* expiration and freshness;  
* replay handling;  
* withdrawal, refusal, rejection, and error behavior;  
* privacy and disclosure fields;  
* extension and profile points;  
* conformance tests.

### 

### **Fiduciary-agent Trust Task profile**

Each fiduciary-agent profile should define, where applicable:

* required authority evidence;  
* duty and policy checks;  
* agreement or other governing-context requirements;  
* required cross-record context;  
* owner-review thresholds;  
* acceptable outcome profiles;  
* required process evidence;  
* local Role Record effects and distributed Verifiable Relationship Record receipts, commitments, or checkpoint effects;  
* disclosure and retention constraints;  
* remediation and escalation requirements.

### 

### **Local deterministic Workflow**

The local deterministic Workflow should define:

* context retrieval;  
* Agent Role and authority evaluation;  
* duty integration;  
* Agreement Object and relationship-state evaluation;  
* linked-record evaluation;  
* human or specialist escalation;  
* capability issuance or refusal;  
* Workspace enforcement;  
* recording and evidence production.

### 

### **Verifiable Trust Agent binding profile**

The protected signing profile should define:

* authenticated Workflow;  
* permitted Agent Role;  
* permitted Verifiable Identifier;  
* exact Trust Task identifier and version;  
* recipient and purpose;  
* payload restrictions;  
* expiration and replay limits;  
* required audit evidence;  
* refusal behavior.

This division allows generic Trust Tasks to remain reusable while fiduciary profiles and local Workflows supply the duties, context, enforcement, and evidence required by accountable agents.

### **6.1 Exact, Versioned Trust Task Identifiers**

Each operation should have a canonical type URI, such as:

https://trusttasks.org/spec/agent/agreement/propose/0.1

The exact identifier should be used throughout the system as:

* the Workflow’s permitted action type;  
* a VTA signing-policy key;  
* a canonical identifier unambiguously bound to the TSP higher-layer message or content type; a conforming profile may use the canonical Trust Task identifier directly as that message type;  
* the counterparty’s dispatch and verification type;  
* the subject of a VTC implementation credential;  
* the event type recorded in the Verifiable Relationship Record;  
* the specification used in a later audit.

A certified Workflow authorized for version `0.1` should not automatically gain authority to invoke a materially different `1.0` or `2.0` task.

A Trust Task should produce a verifiable outcome, but it need not always change persistent relationship state. The task specification or fiduciary profile must state whether the outcome proposes, creates, confirms, refuses, challenges, reverses, or leaves unchanged any agreement or relationship state.

Where applicable, Trust Task profiles should use a common outcome vocabulary:

* accepted;  
* rejected;  
* declined;  
* unsupported;  
* unauthorized;  
* invalid;  
* expired;  
* withdrawn;  
* counterproposed;  
* pending;  
* partially satisfied;  
* escalated;  
* disputed;  
* remediated;  
* superseded.

A verification request may produce evidence without changing the relationship. A rejected proposal may be recorded without activating an agreement. An acceptance may activate one or more agreements. A remediation outcome may alter obligations without restoring an earlier state.

### **6.2 Initial Fiduciary-Agent Ceremony Suite**

The initial suite should define ceremony profiles for:

1. **Solicitation and Calling-Card Review** — Exchange a bounded request for attention, review participant RCards, and determine whether the parties will enter a more consequential ceremony.

2. **Relationship Introduction and Recognition** — Establish appropriate identifiers, communication channels, and any typed Verifiable Relationship Credentials needed to recognize an introduction or other edge.

3. **Fiduciary Compatibility Review** — Determine whether cooperation is permissible, conditional, unsupported, prohibited, or subject to owner or specialist review.

4. **Externality Review and Affected-Party Engagement** — Identify material effects on non-parties and determine whether mitigation, compensation, consultation, representation, redesign, or refusal is required.

5. **Agreement Formation** — Select or construct Agreement Objects; propose, counterpropose, withdraw, reject, or accept exact versions; and satisfy required signatures, approvals, thresholds, and activation conditions.

6. **Owner Review and Authorization** — Produce an understandable Human Review Packet and obtain narrowly scoped authorization where standing authority is insufficient.

7. **Capability Activation** — Translate effective authority and governing terms into narrow technical capabilities and protected signing permissions.

8. **Performance and Compliance Review** — Record or attest significant performance, milestones, exceptions, compliance findings, and unresolved uncertainty.

9. **Challenge, Reconciliation, and Remediation** — Submit challenges, preserve disputed evidence, negotiate correction, obtain adjudication where necessary, and record remediation.

10. **Amendment, Renewal, Suspension, and Closure** — Change future agreement or relationship state without rewriting accepted history.

These ceremonies should be composed from exact Trust Task operations.

 **Initial candidate operations include:**

* request RCard;  
* present or update RCard;  
* withdraw an obsolete RCard;  
* propose ceremony profile;  
* accept, reject, or counterpropose ceremony profile;  
* establish or verify an appropriate TSP Relationship;  
* request a typed Verifiable Relationship Credential;  
* issue, acknowledge, suspend, or revoke a typed Verifiable Relationship Credential;  
* propose Agreement Object;  
* counterpropose Agreement Object;  
* withdraw or reject proposal;  
* accept exact Agreement Object version;  
* attest owner authorization;  
* request capability;  
* issue, attenuate, suspend, expire, or revoke capability;  
* submit process attestation;  
* submit performance or compliance event;  
* challenge recorded assertion;  
* submit correction;  
* propose or accept remedy;  
* record adjudicated outcome;  
* propose amendment;  
* accept renewal;  
* suspend agreement or relationship state;  
* close an agreement, record, or relationship state.

These operations should reuse generic Trust Tasks wherever possible. Fiduciary-agent profiles should add the required authority, duty, owner-review, externality, record-effect, privacy, and evidence requirements rather than duplicating generic protocols.

## **7\. Role Records and Distributed Verifiable Relationship Records**

Role Records form the durable local-state center of the architecture. Distributed Verifiable Relationship Records form the external relationship-evidence layer assembled from relationship-bearing portions of those Role Records and evidence held by other authorized participants. A distributed relationship structure may preserve a relationship before any agreement exists, represent one or more agreements, or provide context for agreements represented through typed links.

It should contain or provide verifiable pointers to:

* persistent record identifier;  
* contributing Role Record roots, relationship-evidence roots, and the latest applicable Relationship Knowledge Checkpoint;  
* prior record states;  
* parties and Agent Roles;  
* principals and beneficiaries;  
* TSP Relationship and VID references;  
* VRCs;  
* current and prior RCards;  
* authority and delegation chains;  
* fiduciary preferences;  
* duties, policies, and precedents;  
* Agreement Objects, if any, including the distinct identity and exact operative version of each agreement;  
* acceptances and activation records;  
* typed relationships among agreements contained within the record;  
* typed links to related Verifiable Relationship Records;  
* the larger Relationship context supplied by those linked records;  
* dependencies, activation conditions, and termination effects among agreements and records;  
* approvals;  
* data-use terms;  
* recording and retention rules;  
* capability grants and revocations;  
* externality assessments;  
* affected-party commitments;  
* Trust Task instances and outcomes;  
* deterministic Workflow versions;  
* VTA signing contexts;  
* process and execution attestations;  
* significant performance events;  
* witnesses, auditors, and certifiers;  
* feedback;  
* complaints and disputes;  
* remediation;  
* reputation evidence;  
* agreement amendment, derivation, implementation, renewal, remediation, supersession, and succession lineage;  
* the terms, duties, authority, capabilities, and obligations inherited or altered through that lineage;  
* the effect of linked agreements on the interpretation and validity of current actions;  
* suspension;  
* closure;  
* surviving obligations.

### **7.1 Agreement Organization, Lineage, and Cross-Record Context**

One materially distinct agreement per Verifiable Relationship Record is the preferred default for functional division, not a mandatory cardinality rule.

**A Verifiable Relationship Record may validly contain:**

* no agreements;  
* one agreement;  
* multiple agreements intentionally governed together;  
* successive versions of an evolving agreement;  
* supplementary or implementing agreements;  
* agreements produced as consequences of earlier agreements;  
* references to agreements governed primarily through other Verifiable Relationship Records.

The relevant parties may agree to govern multiple agreements within one record when consolidation better serves their shared purpose, operational structure, authority model, privacy requirements, compliance needs, or lifecycle management. Each agreement must nevertheless remain separately identifiable and interpretable.

**For every agreement contained within a multi-agreement record, the record should identify:**

* the agreement identifier and exact operative version;  
* its purpose;  
* its parties and their roles;  
* its authority and delegation basis;  
* applicable duties and policies;  
* activation and dependency conditions;  
* capabilities issued under it;  
* performance, compliance, and evidence events attributable to it;  
* its amendment lineage;  
* dispute and remediation state;  
* lifecycle status;  
* its relationship to other agreements inside or outside the record.

Agreements that evolve from, implement, depend upon, or arise as consequences of other agreements require explicit agreement-lineage treatment. Their relationships must not be left to narrative inference.

**Agreement-lineage links should distinguish at least:**

* amends — changes identified terms while preserving the continuity of the agreement;  
* supplements — adds terms without displacing the existing agreement;  
* implements — operationalizes authority, duties, or obligations established by another agreement;  
* is authorized by — derives its legal, fiduciary, organizational, or relational authority from another agreement;  
* is required by — is formed to discharge an obligation created by another agreement;  
* derives from — emerges from another agreement without merely amending it;  
* depends on — remains effective only while another agreement or condition remains effective;  
* remediates — creates corrective duties or remedies following a failure, complaint, or dispute;  
* renews — continues substantially the same arrangement for a new period;  
* supersedes — replaces all or identified portions of an earlier agreement;  
* succeeds — becomes the operative agreement after a predecessor ends;  
* terminates with — cannot survive termination of the linked agreement;  
* survives — remains effective despite completion or termination of the linked agreement.

**Each lineage link should identify:**

* the source agreement and version;  
* the resulting or related agreement and version;  
* the type and direction of the relationship;  
* the authority under which the later agreement was created;  
* the parties whose consent was required;  
* terms, duties, powers, or obligations inherited;  
* terms expressly modified, excluded, or extinguished;  
* activation and dependency conditions;  
* the effect of suspension, completion, or termination of either agreement;  
* the Verifiable Relationship Record or Records governing each agreement;  
* capability, disclosure, retention, compliance, and remediation consequences.

Where agreements are governed through separate Verifiable Relationship Records, typed cross-references allow each agreement to be interpreted within the larger Relationship. The ability to verify that records are linked does not automatically authorize a party to inspect the linked record, traverse all of its links, aggregate its contents, or exercise authority or capabilities established elsewhere.

**A conforming Workflow must therefore apply two complementary rules:**

1. It must not ignore linked context that materially affects an agreement’s meaning, authority, validity, duties, dependencies, or consequences.  
2. It must not infer authority, consent, access, disclosure permission, capability, or shared lifecycle state merely because two agreements or records are linked.

### 

### **7.2 Append-Only Local and Relationship-Evidence Updating**

Previously accepted Role Record transitions, relationship evidence, receipts, and checkpoints should not be silently overwritten.

A correction appends a new event identifying:

* the record corrected;  
* reason;  
* authority;  
* evidence;  
* effect on previous findings;  
* unresolved disagreement.

### **7.3 Practical Persistence**

Role Records and the distributed Verifiable Relationship Record should preserve relationship continuity, not unnecessary detail.

Preserving continuity includes preserving enough typed agreement and record lineage to interpret the current relationship state correctly. It does not require consolidating all linked records, agreements, or evidence into one master dossier.

**It may retain:**

* a hash digest rather than source data;  
* a signed summary rather than a transcript;  
* a deletion attestation rather than deleted content;  
* a protected pointer rather than an exposed record;  
* a proof that review occurred without revealing private reasoning;  
* a commitment that can be selectively disclosed later.

### **7.4 Authorized Relationship Views**

Different parties may receive different Authorized Relationship Views assembled from the distributed Verifiable Relationship Record and its contributing Role Records.

A Relationship View may also include authorized evidence of links to other Verifiable Relationship Records when those links are material to understanding an agreement or the larger Relationship. The view should disclose only the link, context, and supporting information its recipient is authorized to receive. Permission to see one record or one cross-reference does not imply permission to inspect every linked record.

Every material assertion should remain linked to authoritative source records so that redaction does not create unverifiable parallel histories.

## **8\. Security and Sovereignty**

### **8.1 Protecting Against Live Agent Excessive Knowledge**

A Live Agent instantiated in model memory  should not receive unrestricted access to:

* private keys;  
* raw capability tokens;  
* complete policy source;  
* hidden security thresholds;  
* VTA administration;  
* audit-control credentials;  
* Verifiable Relationship Record write authority;  
* protected evidence;  
* every rule used to detect manipulation.

It may receive a bounded explanation:

> The current agreement does not permit publication without owner review.

It need not receive the complete detection logic or security policy.

### **8.2 Preventing Direct Actuation**

The Live Agent does not call arbitrary external tools.

It produces media that a deterministic Workflow may classify into a closed vocabulary of actions.

Unsupported or ambiguous output remains unexecuted.

### **8.3 Protecting Cryptographic Authority**

The embedded VTA wouldn’t expose a general unrestricted arbitrary-signing operation to the Live Agent.

It should support narrowly defined operations bound to:

* authenticated Workflow;  
* certified version;  
* Agent Role;  
* exact Trust Task;  
* VID;  
* recipient;  
* context;  
* payload restrictions;  
* expiration;  
* logging requirements.

### **8.4 Protecting the Workflow from Alteration**

High-assurance implementations should support:

* signed Workflow artifacts;  
* executable digests;  
* read-only deployment;  
* secure boot;  
* remote attestation;  
* protected policy \+ duty versions;  
* separation of deployment and runtime administration;  
* externally visible certification and revocation status.

### **8.5 Protecting VTA State**

The VTA profile would support:

* keys remaining inside protected execution;  
* encrypted persistent state;  
* configuration locking;  
* protected audit events;  
* key rotation;  
* attested software measurements;  
* rollback resistance;  
* fail-closed startup where protected state cannot be verified.

### **8.6 Protecting Role Records and Distributed Verifiable Relationship Records**

Role Record transitions and distributed Verifiable Relationship Record events should be:

* signed;  
* ordered or causally linked;  
* immutable once accepted;  
* externally witnessable where needed;  
* subject to replay checks;  
* resistant to unauthorized deletion or rollback;  
* selectively disclosable.

The ability to verify a record, agreement, event, or typed link must not imply unrestricted access to its contents or to the larger relationship graph.

High-assurance implementations should prevent:

* unauthorized traversal of linked Verifiable Relationship Records;

* aggregation of separately authorized views into a prohibited master dossier;

* inference of hidden relationships from unnecessary identifiers or link metadata;

* reuse of authority or capabilities across record boundaries;

* disclosure of unrelated agreements merely because they share parties;

* concealment of material linked context when that context is required for a legitimate decision.

The architecture must therefore support selective proof of relevant context as well as selective disclosure of record contents.

### **8.7 Sovereignty Does Not Eliminate Interior Boundaries**

The VTA can be inside the user’s sovereign domain while remaining isolated from other internal components.

Sovereignty concerns who ultimately controls and benefits from the system.

Isolation concerns how damage is limited if one component is compromised.

Both are required.

---

### **8.8 Data-Object Capability Profiles and Controlled Use**

A data object’s movement classification should be treated as a type-level Object-Capability profile: a default specification of the operations that may be authorized for objects of that type. Movement does not necessarily mean literal relocation. It includes controlled access, reference, presentation, derivation, execution, retention, propagation, and disclosure.

Three general profiles are useful:

* Anchor: The authoritative source that remains under designated control. Other parties receive references, presentations, verification results, or proofs rather than unrestricted possession of the source object.

* Session: The object may be used within a bounded session, protected Workspace, purpose, recipient set, and duration. Continued retention or reuse requires separate authorization.

* Signal: An authorized assertion, notification, aggregate, recommendation, or derived output may propagate, even where its source information remains local or protected.

These profiles are type-level defaults, not self-enforcing metadata. Actual use requires an instance-level capability derived under the relevant authority, duties, agreement or other governing basis, purpose, recipient, Workspace, and relationship state.

More than one interface may be authorized for the same underlying object. For example, a source record may remain Anchor-controlled while a selective proof is presented within a Session and a permitted derivation is released as a Signal.

For every governed object use, the architecture should preserve a four-part enforcement chain:

1. Policy declaration: the applicable object-use rule is specified.

2. Capability derivation: a narrow capability is derived for a particular operation, party, purpose, and duration.

3. Workspace enforcement: the system technically limits the operation to that capability.

4. Evidence production: sufficient evidence is produced to verify what was authorized and what occurred.

A declaration that an object is Anchor-, Session-, or Signal-type does not by itself enforce the restriction.

## **9\. Verifiable Trust Communities in the Governance Stack**

VTCs make community trust rules machine-verifiable without turning the community into the owner of each participant’s agent.

A Verifiable Trust Community may govern, recognize, certify, witness, or provide recourse for a relationship. It is not automatically a substantive party to, owner of, or constitutor of every relationship formed by its members or under its governance framework.

The architecture distinguishes:

* a Verifiable Trust Community policy or governance rule;

* a credential or attestation issued or recognized by the community;

* a trust-registry publication;

* incorporation of a community rule into an Agreement Object or ceremony profile;

* local deterministic Workflow evaluation of community evidence;

* agreement- or relationship-specific authority given to the community.

A community credential remains evidence until an applicable agreement, authority structure, ceremony profile, or governance framework removes its relevance. Membership does not by itself establish authority for an unrelated action.

A relationship may involve several communities with different functions. One may certify a Workflow, another may recognize a professional role, another may supply dispute resolution, and another may govern a particular shared resource. Local agents must evaluate the relevance, current status, authority, and sufficiency of each community’s evidence.

A Fiduciary Agent VTC might issue or recognize credentials for:

* fiduciary-agent membership;  
* approved duty bundles;  
* Agent Role conformance;  
* Workflow identity and version;  
* Workspace configuration;  
* embedded VTA implementation;  
* approved Trust Task implementations;  
* Agreement Object templates;  
* privacy and data-handling practice;  
* witness, auditor, mediator, or arbitrator status;  
* remediation completion;  
* authority to issue a particular attestation.

An agent Workflow can query a trust registry or verify credentials  before accepting them as evidence.

The VTC may revoke or suspend a certification. Each local agent then determines the effect under its duties and agreements.

A single agent may participate in several VTCs. This supports contextual trust and prevents one community’s policy from becoming a universal authority.

### **9.1 Governance Interfaces**

Governance becomes operational through several interfaces between the Governance and Technology Stacks:

1. Rules and policy profiles define applicable requirements, prohibitions, roles, and procedures.

2. Attribute and role vocabularies give shared meaning to claims, parties, authority, and relationship functions.

3. Credentials, attestations, and registries supply verifiable governance and assurance evidence.
